paragraphs: By the fourth month of the siege of Xiangyang, black flies had begun to breed in the northern trenches.

Some of the dead had been buried; others lay sunk in the water, no more than half a suit of armor showing above the mud. Qin’s third assault had failed. The ram had broken a wheel, and long scaling ladders lay toppled into the ditch. As the autumn sun rose, the stench drifted slowly from the northern wall toward the riverbank, overpowering even the smoke from the millet pots in camp. From the embrasures, Jin soldiers looked down in silence. For three days no one on the wall had laughed.
Fu Pi stood high in a watchtower, gripping the wooden rail until it creaked.
“Bring the dead back tonight.”
The staff officer hesitated. “Forty men went out the night before last. Twenty-three came back. The crossbowmen on the wall know when we enter the ditch.”
“Change their armor. Send five hundred this time.”
“Your Highness, those men are alive too.”

Fu Pi wheeled on him. The officer was young, with a pale scar across his face. Knowing he had spoken out of turn, he was about to kneel when Fu Pi waved him away. “Prepare the large shields. Tell them to drag back as many bodies as they can, but to come back alive themselves.”

Five hundred men went out that night. Before the crossbows opened fire, one soldier found half a boot in the water, its sole worn through in a place he himself had patched before they left Chang’an. Unable to let go, he tied the rope at his waist around the dead man’s arm. Suddenly torches flared on the battlements, and arrows hissed across the darkness. When the retreat sounded, he was still kneeling in the ditch, trying to pull his comrade free. A Qiang soldier beside him sprang forward and cut the rope where it had tangled around dead branches, then seized his head and rolled with him beneath a shield. Both took arrows in the back. Only a little over four hundred came back to camp that night. Fewer than two hundred bodies were recovered.
At dawn Fu Pi ordered another assault.

Officers from the various camps stood in his tent, their wet clothes dripping onto the edges of the felt. A Han captain of siege engineers hid his cracked fingers in his sleeves and reported with evident reluctance, “We have exhausted the timber for battering rams. To build more, we must fell trees in the hills thirty li away. The sacks of earth in the front camp can fill only two shallow ditches.”
“Dismantle the outer camp walls,” Fu Pi said.
“Those walls protect us against attacks at night.”
“Once we take the city, we need fear no night attack.”

The officers lowered their eyes. Their silence only increased Fu Pi’s agitation. He snatched up a brush to write the order, but the tent flap rose. Murong Chui entered in an old sheepskin coat, the damp of the river on his shoulders. He looked first at the assault plan, then at the plate of untouched cold cakes beside it.
“Did Your Highness sleep last night?”
“How could I sleep while the city still stands?”
“Then eat a piece first. A man who gives orders hungry is liable to stake tens of thousands of lives at once.”
Fu Pi did not move. Murong took a cake himself and broke it open. The millet inside had gone so hard that it crumbled between his fingers.
“Have you come to persuade me to abandon the siege?”

“I have come to report something. Someone slipped out of the city last night carrying a sick child and has reached our camp. He says several rice shops by the south gate have closed. Zhu Xu has gathered up the grain in the city. Even the shops that once sold lamp oil are serving gruel now.”
“Xiangyang is running out of food?”
“The garrison still has grain. It is the townspeople who are starving first.”
“Then we should press the assault all the harder.”
Murong laid a deposition on the table. “How many more men do you mean to bury in that ditch?”

All the anger Fu Pi had kept within him broke out. “I have fought here for four months! What am I to say when I return to Chang’an? That the Prince of Changle spent half a year building graves beneath Xiangyang? When you took cities in Hexi, did anyone stand in your way?”

Murong, angered himself, nevertheless kept his voice low. “At Guzang the people inside were willing to open the gates. If Xiangyang remains willing to resist, you could pull down the whole Qin camp and throw it into the ditch, and it would not make the road into the city any shorter.”
“Are we simply to sit here and wait?”

“Draw the troops back first.” Murong spread the map and pointed to a corner in the southeast. “Leave a road open here. Let any townspeople who wish to go come out against a register. Give them water and food, and let them choose where to go. Zhu Xu should know that we besiege him without intending to starve every living soul within his walls.”
Fu Pi gave a cold laugh. “If we let the people go, Zhu Xu will have fewer mouths to feed. He will hold out longer.”
“Perhaps.”
“Then what do you gain?”
“Fewer dead within the walls. If men still wish to defend Zhu Xu, we shall fight the garrison. But if the people carrying ladders and stones no longer wish to stay, Zhu Xu himself will see it.”

Murong made no promise of a glorious victory within three days. Fu Pi looked at the sick child’s symptoms recorded in the deposition and suddenly remembered another young face in the ditch the previous night. He snapped the bamboo brush in his hand and ordered the fourth assault suspended. They would repair the camp, recover bodies, and put the grain road in order first. When word reached the ranks, several men already armored for the attack sank down against a timber post. Some laughed; others buried their faces against their knees. It was impossible to tell whether they were exhausted or weeping.
That same day, the people of Xiangyang were also collecting their dead.

Zhu Xu had not taken off his armor. His shoulders were white with lime dust fallen from the wall. The chief clerk reported that the granary could still feed the soldiers, but households in several wards had gone without cooking fires. Qin troops had blocked two old channels in the southern city. There were plenty of wells, but women carrying water now had farther to walk. When he had heard the figures, Zhu Xu ordered his own ration halved and the remainder sent to the families of the wounded.
His deputy tried to dissuade him. “If you eat so little, Governor, you will not have the strength to inspect the walls tomorrow.”
“Some have no tomorrow left to them.”

He said it without emphasis. His deputy knew better than to argue and instructed the kitchen accordingly. Zhu Xu then climbed the western wall. He saw the gate of a house broken down. Its owner had hung an old mat across the entrance, while his daughter-in-law, heavy with child, picked grains of millet from among the bricks that had not been crushed underfoot. A girl of five or six was helping her. Whenever her hand reached near a soldier’s boot, she snatched it back in fright.

Zhu Xu placed his dry ration on the stone steps and ordered his guards to bring water. The child dared not take it. She knew the bright red cloak he wore. Only the day before, people in the city had been saying that the governor would have anyone caught hoarding grain whipped. Looking at her tightly clenched hand, Zhu Xu felt a shame he could not put into words.

A few days later the Qin soldiers outside the southeast gate moved back their palisade, leaving a gap that opened onto the roads to the rivers south and west. Small white flags stood at intervals of a hundred paces. A notice tied to an arrow was shot over the wall: civilians leaving the city would not be searched, stripped of possessions, or seized for military service. Soldiers attempting to leave among them must declare themselves and submit to inspection.
Zhu Xu held the notice for a long while without speaking. His deputy urged him to burn it.
“Who has seen it?”
“The men on the wall. Some of the people nearby as well.”
“Then what good would burning it do?”

That evening people gathered at the southern gate, begging leave for their old parents and sick children to depart. The officer on duty dared not decide and ordered them away. An old woman knelt before him. Two of her sons had died on the northern wall; the last was still drawing a crossbow there. If she could not send her grandson away, she said, there might be no one left to tend the family’s ancestral offerings. The officer answered harshly and rode around her. Yet on his return he stood half the night outside Zhu Xu’s residence.

At last Zhu Xu permitted the small southeastern gate to be opened at fixed times, the sick, women, children, and elderly leaving first. Those who wished to stay were not to be driven out; soldiers were not to slip away under cover of the evacuation. Each day before the gate opened, he inspected the watch posts in person. He feared the Qin might rush in through the crowd. He feared just as much that his own defenders would scatter while escorting their families.

Only a little over a hundred went out the first day. Some reached the white flags and turned back at the sight of Qin spears stretched across the road in the distance. Several times as many left on the second day. One woman carried the family’s last copper cooking pot; beneath her headcloth she had wrapped her grandfather’s memorial tablet. An old craftsman had taken the iron ring from his front door and held it close inside his coat. Even at the relief shelter he kept touching it, as though afraid he might have lost the entrance to his home upon the road.

Fu Pi inspected the receiving parties himself. The clerks had divided the civilians into columns: those bound for kin in Jin territory, those temporarily remaining in Nanyang, those in need of physicians, and those separated from their families. Some refused to give their names and asked only for water. Some cursed Qin, saying none of their families would have been forced to flee had Xiangyang not been besieged. Fu Pi endured it and ordered food issued as before.
“They have plenty of strength to curse us,” one of his officers said bitterly. “Zhu Xu took their grain inside the city, and they still come out blaming Qin.”

Fu Pi did not answer. He stopped beside an ox cart. A wooden horse caked with mud was tied to the shaft, one of its legs broken. When the child holding it saw Fu Pi’s horse approaching, she clutched the toy tightly. Her mother began to prostrate herself, but Fu Pi raised a hand to stop her and rode on.

After a dozen more days, over twenty thousand civilians had left. Whole wards of Xiangyang stood empty, while the bowls of the remaining garrison were fuller than before. Walking along the eastern street, Zhu Xu no longer heard carts being repaired or meat being chopped. Passing an abandoned house, he heard the wind slapping its unremoved window paper against the frame. The farther he went through the empty lanes, the harder Murong Chui’s tactic became to bear. With no crying children and no old people carrying stones, the soldiers who remained heard only their own footsteps ringing through deserted streets. Some began asking where the relief army from Jiangling could be.
During one night patrol, Zhu Xu found words written in charcoal upon the wall: IF THE REINFORCEMENTS COME, WILL THEY STILL FIND US HERE?

He ordered the words erased. The soldier assigned to do it was seventeen, his hands trembling so badly that he took a long while to scrub them away. Zhu Xu did not punish him. He asked where the boy’s parents were. They had left through the southeast gate three days earlier. Zhu Xu patted his shoulder, sent him to rest, and took the torch himself to continue the patrol.

It was then that Li Bohu, the commander of the western wall, secretly opened a channel to Qin. At first he asked only where his wife and children had gone after leaving the city. The Qin registration clerk told him they were safe in Nanyang, waiting to join relatives. Then he asked whether surrendered soldiers would be sold as slaves. The messenger brought him a copy of Fu Jian’s order forbidding plunder and said the fate of the twenty-odd households that had fled earlier could be checked. Li Bohu did not wholly believe him. He was a man of Xiangyang. Nearly every lane, shop, and family within its walls bore a name he knew. If he brought Qin into the city and even one of those people died, someone would ask him about it for the rest of his life.
After several exchanges, he finally asked about Zhu Xu himself.
“If I open the gates, what will become of Governor Zhu?”
“Our orders are to take him alive and send him to Chang’an for questioning,” the Qin envoy said. “General Murong has forbidden us to kill him.”
“Will you keep your word?”
The envoy pointed to the military registration badge at his waist. “I cannot pledge that piece of wood for another man’s word. But remember my name. If things go wrong, you will know whom to find.”

Li Bohu held the copied decree a long time before folding it into his sleeve. Several days later he removed two company captains from the western wall with whom he had long been at odds, replacing them with veterans loyal to him. It was the ugliest thing he had ever done, and perhaps one he would never again dare remember.
On the night the western gate fell, the autumn rain was as fine as mist.

Three short horn blasts sounded across the city. Zhu Xu had just laid his armor beside the couch when a guardsman shouted that the west gate was burning. He threw on his armor, fastening the belt through the wrong loop, and hurried to the street. Li Bohu’s men had already cut one of the gate ropes. The drawbridge dropped askew across the ditch. Qin shield-bearers came over it, short spears in the front rank, water skins and torches carried behind. Their horses stayed outside; no cavalry surged through the opening.
In the gateway Zhu Xu met Li Bohu. The two men who had defended Xiangyang together stood facing one another through rain and firelight.
“You opened it?” Zhu Xu asked.
Blood marked Li Bohu’s shoulder armor. He nodded.
“Your family has already gone.”
“Many other families are still here.”
“Have I ever denied you grain?”
Li Bohu’s eyes reddened. “You have never wronged me, Governor. I am afraid that if we hold out until winter, Xiangyang will contain nothing but soldiers and graves.”

Zhu Xu seemed about to reply, but the Qin shield wall was closing behind Li Bohu. He drew his sword and shouted for his guards to retake the gate. Dozens of Jin soldiers charged into the passage, trampling over old blood only to meet the cold iron of Qin. A guardsman went down under a spear. Zhu Xu swung his blade to help him, striking the rim of a shield and notching his sword. Murong Chui had strictly ordered him taken alive. Qin soldiers gave ground by two paces and caught his sword between their spear shafts instead. At several street corners men shouted, “Lay down your arms and live!” Jin soldiers still fired arrows from rooftops, but others, after half a year under siege, threw their spears into the rainwater and sat with their backs against the walls.

Zhu Xu retreated as far as the inner city. His last bodyguard died at the steps. A sword cut had opened his left arm; half his sleeve was soaked with blood, but he still held the blade. Over the western gate he saw a Qin unit flag rising. The rain plastered the cloth to the pole, and for a long while it would not unfurl.
“Governor Zhu,” a Qin captain said as he approached, “please lay down your sword. The general has ordered that no harm come to you.”

Zhu Xu looked down at the chip in the blade. There were civilians who had not left and thousands of soldiers hiding in ruined houses and passages inside the walls. If he died now, no one would remain to order those men to stop fighting.

“I will go with you.” He slowly opened his hand and released the hilt. “First carry my order to the garrison. Every Xiangyang unit is to lay down its arms. No burning the granaries. No harm to the households in the streets.”
The captain did not delay. He called for paper and had the order written down on the spot.

When the news of the city’s fall reached Fu Pi’s table, he stared for a long while. Months earlier he had drawn three red lines of approach on the assault plan, thinking night and day about where he would first scale the walls. Yet on the night the city was taken he heard only that Murong Chui had entered through the west gate. There had not even been a single beat of the war drum for an army-wide assault.
“Form up and enter the city.” He seized his sword and finally raised his voice. “Secure the warehouses and the water gates first.”

Too many troops entered at once and crowded the narrow streets. The men at the front smelled wine; those behind heard only shouts that the city had fallen. Some cried that their fathers and brothers had died in the northern ditch and that taking a single jar of wine was the least they were owed for their rites. Others rushed a house, certain that Jin military grain was hidden there. As the door was smashed with a pole, an old woman fell from within and clutched a soldier’s leg, weeping.
“There are no soldiers in my house,” she said.

Fu Pi rode to the lane and saw three men dragging out a wooden chest, with others carrying bolts of cloth. His officers pressed him to permit a reward. “Let them take some wine, Your Highness. Just for tonight.”

For one instant he gave no answer. By the time he reached out to stop them, the first wine jar had shattered on the paving, and men rushed toward the smell. Matters often turn upon a commander’s single moment of silence. Fu Pi drew his sword, the scabbard striking his horse’s neck and startling it. He was about to order the troops back when the military-law gong sounded from the west. Three heavy beats rang through the cries filling the street.
Murong Chui had arrived with the military-police battalion.

He made no long speech. He raised Fu Jian’s decree and ordered the cavalry on both sides to dismount and unstring their bows, sealing the lane. Military judges called the rolls unit by unit and collected the wine and cloth that had been taken. One man resisted with his sword and stabbed a comrade sent to arrest him. He was killed there by the military-law soldiers. Officers who had still been thinking of joining the disorder saw the body and finally ordered their men back into ranks. A Qin soldier caught dragging a chest was pinned to the ground, still shouting that his brother had died in the northern ditch and asking why he must leave empty-handed.
“Your brother’s name is in the army registers,” Murong Chui told him.
“Can a register bring him back?”
“No. I have commanded more dead men than you have ever seen.”
“Then why may I not take even one piece of cloth?”
Murong looked toward a child crouching inside the house. “Did anyone in that household kill your brother?”
The soldier said nothing. The cords stood out along his temples. Murong ordered him taken back to camp to await judgment. Just then Fu Pi came riding down the lane.

“All units, heed the orders of the Prince of Changle!” Fu Pi shouted, his voice raw from smoke. “No entering private homes without orders. No taking possessions, no violation of women, no killing prisoners. Anything seized tonight must be returned to its place. Those who have hurt people in defiance of the decree will answer under military law.”

Murong glanced at him and slowly lowered the decree. Fu Pi knew that he had spoken too late. He knew too that some clerk would one day record that pause in the military-law register, with no blank space left for the moment merely because he was the Heavenly King’s son.

That night guards were posted in every ward and street, the granaries sealed, and wounded soldiers gathered in two temple hostels. The military-law battalion arrested dozens for unauthorized looting. Those guilty of the gravest crimes were executed under military orders; the rest were detained pending examination. Not every confiscated possession could be returned. A bronze mirror passed from hand to hand, its back engraved with two small characters, but the family name had been rubbed away. One chest of cloth was mixed with several military vouchers. A clerk copied the inventory three times and still could not find anyone to claim two of the objects. Women and children in the city did not dare sleep. Weeping sounded by the wells, the stables, and half-collapsed houses through the night and had not quite ceased by dawn.

When Fu Pi inspected the eastern street, the child with the wooden horse was there. She and her mother had come back from the relief shelters outside the walls after hearing that one room of their home remained. At the corner a fallen Jin flag lay across the road, the wind blowing its torn cloth against the girl’s feet. She stepped over it without knowing what it was, thinking only of the old door with its iron ring.
Three days after the battle, Fu Pi met Zhu Xu.

Zhu Xu wore no shackles. His old armor had been removed, and white cloth bound the wound on his left arm. He greeted them according to Jin custom; Fu Pi did not compel him to kneel. For a while they faced one another across the table. Fu Pi spoke first. “The city has fallen.”
“I heard.”
“The western gate was opened by one of your own commanders.”
“I saw that too.”
Fu Pi had meant to speak further about victory and defeat, but suddenly could find no words. Instead he asked, “How many of your men are still hiding in the city?”

Zhu Xu named several cellars where old weapons had been stored and asked the Qin to seal them before soldiers seeking revenge forced their way in. Murong ordered it done and arranged for Zhu Xu to stay in his former residence under guard. He was not to leave without permission, but could continue to wear the garments of his former station.
“You were once a prince of Yan,” Zhu Xu said to Murong. “Now you have helped Qin take Jin land. If one day an army comes to seize Ye, what would you wish to do?”

Fu Pi frowned. Murong said nothing for a while. He turned the half-tiger tally between his fingers twice before replying, “I still remember the streets of Ye. But today people in this city need rice, and soldiers need burial. I shall see to those two things first.”

Zhu Xu looked at him and asked no more. At the mention of rice, Fu Pi ordered the city’s stores registered separately from the grain brought from Nanyang. The wounded and households without food were to receive supplies first. An officer of the finance department protested that the army itself had little grain to spare. Fu Pi remembered his father’s injunction that the main force return north within two months. “We took the city,” he said. “If its people starve, the report will bear my name.”

On the third day the market drum sounded again. Few doors opened. The lamp-oil shop first lifted half a shutter; beside it an apothecary hung out a small wooden board saying that herbs were scarce and only people with old wounds would be treated. Qin soldiers repaired the broken winding wheel over a well. The flag upon the city wall had changed. As Fu Pi rode past, the woman whose house had been broken into still kept her door closed. Only a child looked at him through the crack, her eyes bright but without joy.
He waited a moment, then ordered the soldiers beside him to lift a broken roof beam blocking the entrance. Only after they had gone did the child open the door a little wider.
Qin banners already stood above the walls of Xiangyang. The doors within would have to be opened one by one.
